title: Against the Ropes
full_review:
A brassy female fight fan tosses her hat and her hopes into the ring when she decides to manage a promising young boxer in the leaden "Against the Ropes" (Paramount).

According to press notes, director Charles S. Dutton�s film is �inspired by� the real-life exploits of femme boxing manager Jackie Kallen. But it has little chance of scoring an emotional knockout thanks to deficient performances and a script that doesn't pack much of a punch.

Meg Ryan stars as Kallen, a 36-year-old Detroit native practically raised in the ring, working as a Girl Friday for the director of the Cleveland Coliseum (Joe Cortese). Shooting her mouth off in a local watering hole, she finds herself in a verbal sparring match with Sam LaRocca (Tony Shalhoub), a mob-connected fight promoter, over the role of women in the male-dominated world of professional boxing. She insists women can do more than prance around in bikinis holding round cards.

Through a twist of fate she crosses paths with Luther Shaw (Omar Epps), a young ghetto thug with fire in his eyes, as well as his fists. Recognizing a diamond in the rough, Kallen convinces Shaw to let her manage him. She recruits an old-school trainer (Dutton) to mold Shaw from a street scrapper into a prizefighter.

Her gamble pays off and Shaw quickly climbs through the ranks only to find his way to a title match barred by LaRocca. Furious over being shown up by a woman, LaRocca dangles the middleweight belt like a carrot before Shaw, planting seeds of suspicion in the fighter's head by questioning Kallen's self-promotion and using her swelling celebrity status as a wedge to sour their success.

Together with last year's execrable "In the Cut," this dud forms a one-two punch that could put Ryan's career down for the count. Unlike "In the Cut," however, Ryan manages to keep her clothes on, mostly because they are so skin-tight that removing them would require surgery. Complementing her ridiculous hooker couture is an equally outlandish accent, whose unidentifiable tonality swerves between Brooklyn and Boston.

Like the more serious-minded "Erin Brockovich," the don't-judge-a-walking-fashion-faux-pas-by-its-cover film shoots for a feel-good emotional warmth, but leaves viewers feeling cold. The only thing Ryan's performance will make her a "contender" for is this year's Razzie Award.

Ryan's undercard of Epps and Dutton do their best with the stock roles they are given. Epps is convincing as the passionate pugilist. Dutton, meanwhile, spends most of the film barking motivational maxims from Burgess Meredith's "Handbook of Crusty Trainer Cliches."

Despite Michael Kamen's go-for-it score, the uninspired fight sequences lack any real drama, a consequence which has less to do with the actual choreography than it does with the script's lack of character development. The forced dialogue sounds as if the screenwriter was punch-drunk while writing it. The film really shows its narrative glass jaw during the hackneyed ringside pep talk during the climactic title fight.

"Against the Ropes" tries to promote a positive message about self-discovery, loyalty and inner greatness. Sadly, while there may be greatness in each of us, there is not much in this movie.
Due to boxing action, brief violence and drug content, and recurring crude sexual language and humor, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
